38491-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-98:
Notes and Queries for the thirteenth of September 1851 is number ninety-eight of a weekly paper of literary exchange. Its sub-title calls it a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto is Captain Cuttle's rule: when found, make a note of. The price was threepence. This number's notes treat heads from Dr Wotton to Essex's expedition to Ireland. Grimsdyke, surplices, and a passage in Luther stand in the list.

Minor queries are answered in a second rank: the willow garland, the name of a nun, a nine days' wonder. Replies fill the rest of the number. Visiting cards, sardonic smiles, Darby and Joan, and the marriage of bishops all get their answers. The paper was a great Victorian web of shared learning. Its numbers are still mined for lore.
39135-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-10:
Notes and Queries, number 107, is a weekly issue dated Saturday, November 15, 1851. The journal called itself a medium of communication for literary men, artists, and antiquaries. Genealogists also used its pages to trade facts and questions. Its motto, borrowed from Captain Cuttle, ran: when found, make a note of. The price was threepence, or fourpence for the stamped edition.

Inside, readers will find notes on Perkin Warbeck and a Hebrew sermon in stone. Folk lore items treat the ash tree and souling customs. Queries ask about a Roman funeral pile and the Dacres of the north. Replies take up the Caxton Memorial and an epigram ascribed to Mary Queen of Scots. Minor queries cover word origins, old families, and cross legged effigies. The issue shows how Victorian scholars crowdsourced their learning in print.
39197-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-10:
Notes and Queries called itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries and genealogists. Volume four, number 108, appeared on Saturday, November 22, 1851, at threepence. Captain Cuttle's motto, 'When found, make a note of,' heads the title page of the number.

The age of trees leads the notes in this issue's contents list. Lines attributed to Admiral Byng and a chapter on emblems follow in the notes. Folk lore brings music at funerals and Cheshire superstition, while minor notes chase anagrams and hackneyed quotations, with queries on masters of the ceremonies closing the page.
39233-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-10:
Notes and Queries was a week book where men of letters swapped facts. The issue of November 29, 1851 is of its fourth year of print. Its full name calls it a way for such men to trade notes. Small asks and short notes from its readers fill its leaves.

A man might ask who first used a phrase or where a grave lies. An other might tell of a rare book or an old rite of a town. The charm of the book is the mix of the grave and the odd in it. Prints of old songs, word roots, and church lore stand side by side. The book was a post box and a store house for the bookish world. Much of its stuff is the raw ore from which big works are made.
39438-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-11:
The hosted text is one weekly number of Notes and Queries, volume four, number 112, dated Saturday, December 20, 1851. The paper calls itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and students of family history. It cost threepence. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, is: when found, make a note of.

The notes in this number begin with a piece placing Wady Mokatteb in the Bible lands. A note on a passage in Goldsmith follows. Such short pieces were the heart of the paper. Readers sent in finds, puzzles, and answers to each other's questions. The queries and replies that fill the rest of the number range over books, words, old customs, and points of history, in the same brief form.
39503-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-11:
Notes and Queries, number 113, closed volume four on Saturday, December 27, 1851. The weekly still called itself a means of talk among literary men, artists, antiquaries, and family historians, and it still sold for threepence. Its motto stayed the same: when found, make a note of it.

Notes in this number treat chance likenesses in history, the remains of King James the Second, and Shetland folk lore on elfshot, burns, and ringworm. Queries ask the sense of old words, the green-eyed monster, Moravian hymns, and legal time. Answers settle points on Jeremy Taylor, Bacon as a poet, Weever's funeral book, and a motto at Karlsbad. The year's end finds the exchange as busy as ever.
44678-the-penitente-moradas-of-abiquiu:
The Penitente Moradas of Abiquiú is a study by Richard Ahlborn, issued by the Smithsonian Institution Press in 1968. It forms paper 63 in a museum series on history and technology. The government printing office in Washington sold it for seventy-five cents. Its sections treat the brotherhood, the town, and the buildings in turn.

By the early nineteenth century, Spanish-speaking villagers of northern New Mexico felt a need. They formed a brotherhood to keep their old social and religious ways. Known as brothers of light, or penitentes, they centred their life in a morada. That houselike building held their Holy Week ceremonies each year. At Abiquiú, a rural village of the region, two such moradas stood intact. Ahlborn describes their earthen fabric and their special furnishings in detail. A carved cross from the south morada serves as the frontispiece.
49032-bloody-beaches-the-marines-at-pele:
Bloody Beaches is an official history booklet on the Marines at Peleliu, written by Gordon Gayle, a retired brigadier general of the Marine Corps. It belongs to the Marines in World War Two commemorative series. Peleliu, in the Palau Islands, was taken in the autumn of 1944 at heavy cost.

The contents follow the battle in order. First come the Japanese defenses, built into caves and ridges, and the assault across the reef. Sidebars explain the divisions and their commanders, the new Japanese tactics, and the naval gunfire support. The fight in the center, the destruction of the enemy in the south, and the slow encirclement of the Umurbrogol pocket fill the middle chapters. The book ends by asking whether the seizure of Peleliu was necessary, and weighs the costs against the benefits. Paintings by Tom Lea, who landed with the troops, are treated in a sidebar.
britannica-1911-chang-chun-kiu:
Kiu Chang Chun, a Chinese sage of the Taoist faith who lived from 1148 to 1227, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In 1219 the Mongol conqueror Jenghiz Khan wrote to ask him to come and teach him. The Khan's letter is kept, and it shows the fierce chief in a meek and humble mood.

The sage set out from his home in Shantung in 1220. He crossed Mongolia, the Altai hills, and the rich Ili valley on his long road west. At last he reached the Khan's camp near the Hindu Kush. His pupil's tale of the trip gives sharp, true pictures of the lands between the Great Wall and Kabul. It draws the Mongols and the folk of Samarkand with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-nikiu:
John of Nikiu was an Egyptian chronicler of the late seventh century whose history preserves the Arab conquest of Egypt. Little is known of him beyond Severus of Ashmunein's History of the Patriarchs. He served under three patriarchs, became Bishop of Nikiu in the Delta and general administrator of Egypt's monasteries. He was then deposed by Patriarch Simeon after disciplining a monk so harshly that he died ten days later.

His Chronicle, written before his deposition, runs from Adam to the Arab conquest. Often copying Byzantine chroniclers such as Malalas and John of Antioch, it still preserves Egyptian traditions. It gives details on the fall of Phocas, the accession of Heraclius, seventh-century Egypt, and the Arab conquest itself, told little after the events. Written in Greek with Coptic chapters on Egypt, it survives only in an Ethiopic version made in 1602 from a lost Arabic text.
podcast-dannyjones-QJiYc-6XcIU:
The researcher known as UAP Gerb joins Danny Jones to discuss deep sea alien bases and what he calls the underwater CIA project no one talks about. His case assembles naval reports, sonar lore, and declassified fragments into a claim that the oceans hide both non-human occupants and the American programs watching them.

Jones follows the evidence piece by piece, asking which documents exist and which are rumored. The documented core here is thin and the construction on top of it is Gerb's, preserved as his presentation. The ocean setting does real work in the argument: most of the seafloor is unmapped, so absence of evidence feels weaker there. Listeners fascinated by the underwater turn in UFO culture get one of its main researchers laying out the full claim, in the depths where verification goes to die.
podcast-tuckercarlson-XwBMKwt14IU:
John Kiriakou, a former CIA officer who went to prison for leaking, joins Tucker Carlson for a long interview. The title lists the CIA torture program, MK-Ultra, and the attacks of September 11. It also asks why President Obama sent him to jail.

Kiriakou tells how he helped catch terror suspects, then broke ranks over torture. He explains his leak, his trial, and his time in prison in his own words. Carlson draws out his views on the agency he once served. Listeners get a rare first hand account from a man who paid a high price for speaking out.
